instruction.what: Step 3.2, the behaviours of the collection (stage 4, C2), read once every subgroup is through 3.1 and the sweep has closed 3.1: which behaviours of the inner being the collection shows, DISCOVERED from the element observations of its subgroups. The input is the 3.1 findings of the current subgroups (`to_take_up`), each whole with its subgroups and occurrences, not the verses. A behaviour gathers elements; it is never a claim about what the behaviour is (that is stage 5).
read: Apply IB-08 (what a behaviour is). Read every operation finding first, across all the subgroups (`subgroups` lists the findings on each), and write down its core operation in a few words, ignoring the word used for it: who or what does what.

Put together the operation findings whose core operation is the same, even where they sit in different subgroups: the subgroups were made from the dictionary meaning of the words (stage 2), the behaviours from what the elements show the person doing.

Attach to each group the other findings (object, polarity, enactment, role, circumstance, chain) that describe the same verses and the same act: each goes with the operation it describes, not with its subgroup.
Test each group against IB-08: one operation? A group that holds two operations is split; two groups that hold one operation are joined.
Name each behaviour by what is done, never by what it means for the inner being (stage 5).

Read across the behaviours for what relates them: a chain from one into another, a party that acts on several (with its route, B:72), a dimension that runs through several (pursuit or refusal), a circumstance named in several.

Every finding is in exactly one behaviour, or declared not gathered with its reason: the not gathered are those that show no working of a human inner being (another being in its own right, route A; a word that is not an act of the mind). Go back to a verse only where the findings do not settle a question, and say why (read_back).
write: Fill `answer.findings`. Each behaviour is a finding of the item flag (`parts.item` flag, `parts.flag_type` discovery, `kind` statement) that names the behaviour, says which elements belong together and why, and gathers its element observations by a `traced` node on each. At least one behaviour, or `disposition` none with its reason.

What relates elements across subgroups is a finding of operation (with its mode), chain (kind link), party (with the route, B:72), circumstance or role, each resting on the observations it relates by traced nodes.

Every finding also has `occurrence` nodes, with their `role`, on occurrences the observations it rests on cover (each observation's `occurrences`); an occurrence outside them needs a `read_back` entry {verse: the osis id, why}.
`not_gathered`: {observation id: reason} for every observation to take up that no finding rests on. Every one is rested on or declared, never both.
`older`: answer each older unsettled observation on an occurrence your findings name (keep, restate, merge, consume, delete_neither, defer, carry).
The text says what the observations show; it names its verses; it never restates a verse and never formulates the claim.
Then: Collection-Build.ps1 -Action RecordBehaviours -File <the answer file> (-Check to preview). The record refuses the whole file on any fault and lists every fault.

keep.text: Stage 4 starts from the observations, not the verses (researcher, #2526 Q7, 2026-11-21): the subgroups and the stage 3 observations on them are the input, the behaviours are discovered from analysing them, and the base data is read back into only occasionally. Every finding of step 3.1 or 3.2 rests on named observations (a traced node on each, with an occurrence node as well) and its occurrence nodes lie within the occurrences those observations cover; an occurrence outside them is allowed only where the finding records a read-back (the verse and why). Each node has a role from reading.node_roles other than lexical, chosen by the reading. A 3.3 finding carries nodes on the occurrences of both sides in the shared verses.

A finding of a stage 4 row is checked by the rules of observationrecord.check and check_item_parts (kind, text, basis, route, parts.item and what the item needs, node roles, collection of each node) and by RG, RW and RS, which are not restated here: one observation for each finding, never a duplicate, with a node on each word it applies to (RO11, RW-03); founded in the observations and never a restatement of the verse (B:131); parts.item is one of the items the row's item uses (cfg_setting layer.reading). An observation whose nodes all bear on an act is refused: those words are nodes of the observation of the act. A finding is a building block of a behaviour and never a claim (stage 5).

Nothing the step reads is lost on the way to stage 5. Step 3.1: every stage 3 observation of the subgroup is rested on by a finding or declared in not_used with its reason in words. Step 3.2: every 3.1 observation of the collection is gathered into a behaviour (a traced node on it from a flag finding of type discovery) or declared in not_gathered with its reason, and the row has at least one behaviour unless it is recorded as none with its reason. A behaviour names and gathers; it makes no claim about what the behaviour is.

LayerCheck validates a stage 4 row from the tables alone: the demanded occurrences and the observations the row may rest on are re-derived; at least one live observation of stage layer-3 with its stable_key on the row; each observation's parts still valid and its item one the row uses; each live node has a valid role, a collection and its subgroup; each observation has a traced node on an observation the row may rest on; in 3.1 and 3.2 each occurrence node lies in the occurrences of the observations it rests on or its verse is in the recorded read-back; the completeness of IB-04 (not_used, not_gathered, the behaviour of 3.2); no observation restates a run of the verse longer than reading.observation_items max_verse_words_copied. A row that fails is unvalidated and its step is not closed.

Every live observation marked inner_being holds at least one live traced node on a live observation marked evidence, unless it is recorded self-evidencing: it quotes its verse in full and holds a word node for every word it relies on. A traced node never points at a deleted observation. A trace points first at existing evidence; an evidence observation is created only when none states the fact and it states what the nodes and the quotation do not. An inner-being observation traced to evidence not yet marked is pending, not failed.

A behaviour (step 3.2) is one working of the inner being: one core operation, who or what does what, shown by several element observations of 3.1. Elements that show the same operation belong to one behaviour, whatever their mode, polarity, object, party or circumstance, and in whatever subgroup they sit; those differences are written as relating findings (operation, chain, party, circumstance, role). Different operations linked in sequence are a chain between behaviours, not one behaviour. A group that holds two operations is split; two groups that hold one operation are joined. An element that shows no working of a human inner being (another being in its own right, route A of B:72; a word that is not an act of the mind) is declared not gathered with its reason. A behaviour is named by what is done, never by what it means for the inner being (stage 5).

Find the main inner-being operation, and give every word that bears on it its role in this finding (cfg_setting reading.node_roles): characteristic, qualifier and what it gives the characteristic, object or content, relational target, or enactment. A word read in the verse that holds nothing for the inner being is standalone. The role comes from this verse, never from the cluster tag. Where a standalone word proves to qualify a characteristic, it is a qualifier of it.

A qualifier gets no separate account of itself, but what it gives the characteristic it binds to is evaluated for its value and recorded as a qualification finding, applied by its nodes to the qualifier (role qualifier) and the characteristic (role characteristic). What it gives can vary widely: grade, nature, impact, size, relation, a measure, strengthening, ground, cause, object, setting or bait are examples, not a list (#2273 D9). A qualifier whose usage varies across contexts may earn its own reading later.

Record the parties: who bears the act, who causes it, who is acted on (source, target, impact, purpose), and the route (cfg_enum observation_route), whose meaning is cfg_behaviour_rule 72 (route-verses-hib-other-beings-data-only): A another being in its own right, B another being with the human inner being, C no bearing, data only; a verse may take A and B. A non-human being is never itself a HIB; a collective stays one HIB; an implied party is named as referential, never asserted.
Never close a verse or item on 'not X'. A role label is never a verdict; the close records what the verse is. Silence about the inner being is a finding, recorded as data with its reason.
A phenomenon hidden behind a stated or refrained act may be named, with the verb, clause or stated silence that grounds it, and whether it is stated or read.
Keep the source of an interior state apart from the source of an enablement to act.
One observation per finding, never a duplicate description; a finding applying to several verses or words carries several nodes, each with the word's role in it.
One observation per finding: the same description is never written twice. Applied to another verse, word or scope it gains a node on the existing observation.
Observation text is concise and tied to this verse's content, never a restatement of the word's dictionary sense. A transliteration is never given without its gloss.

An observation is created with its marker (ib_observation.nature, from the item answered, cfg_setting layer.reading items.<item>.nature; a finding file never sets it) and every word node with the columns of layer.reading node_required. A column the data cannot give (layer.reading node_gap_columns: an empty morph in the source row, a surface with no placement in the collection index) is left empty and its reason is kept on the node (disposition_note); any other missing column refuses the whole file and nothing is written. A trace to a deleted observation is refused (IB-07).

Evidence states what the data are or show, tied to a verse. Inner being states how something works in the inner being, based on evidence, a building block of the stage 5 claims. The marker (ib_observation.nature) follows the content and purpose of the observation, never its stage (RS-04): an observation of any stage may be inner being when it traces to evidence. One that states both is split. The marker is set when the observation is created, by the item that is answered (cfg_setting layer.reading items.<item>.nature); a finding file never sets it; the validation changes it only where the content shows the item's nature does not hold.

The study's primary focus is the human inner being (HIB). Each verse read is routed by what it shows, and the route is recorded in its observation. (A) Other beings in their own right: a word used of God, angels, other spirits or nature (non-HIB) is routed to Ch 13 "Other beings" (13.1 Divine, 13.2 Angels, 13.3 Other spirits, 13.4 Nature), read for what the verses say that being is and does; for God, also how his character passed to the HIB through creation in his image, held open (#1984). (B) Another being interacting with the HIB is fully in HIB scope. A verse may take A and B, described from different angles. (C) A verse with no inner-being and no other-being bearing is still assessed and recorded as data, and does not enter the narrative.

asks: Which behaviours does this collection show, discovered from the element observations of its subgroups? A behaviour may be one subgroup, part of one, or gather elements from several; a subgroup may form none. Record each behaviour as a finding of the item flag with flag_type discovery that names it and gathers its element observations by a traced node on each, saying which elements belong together and why; it states no claim about what the behaviour is (stage 5). Record also, as findings of operation, chain, party, circumstance or role, what relates elements across subgroups. Every 3.1 observation of the collection is gathered into a behaviour or declared not gathered, with the reason. Where the collection shows no behaviour, record none with its reason.

uses.name: a typed flag: data-quality, or discovery for the claims process
the operation as an action description (who or what does what), its mode, the primary one
the chain of operations the verse links in sequence
the other party and the sequence, with the route
how it appears here: the circumstance of the verse
its role: the qualifier and what it gives the characteristic

to_take_up.text: In Rom 2:15 conflicting thoughts are reasonings within a person that argue with one another: the person does it, in himself, as an inner debate.
In Rom 2:15 the reasonings accuse the person or else excuse him: the working takes the part of a judge over the self, in either direction.
In Rom 2:15 the reasonings work beside the conscience, which bears witness, and the heart, on which the work of the law is written: heart, conscience and reasonings are named together.
In Pro 16:20 giving thought is attention with insight turned to the word: the person does it, and it is set as a way of life beside trusting in the Lord.
In Pro 16:20 what the attention is turned to is the word.
In Pro 16:20 attending to the word leads on: the one who does it will find good, as the one who trusts in the Lord is blessed.
In Psa 1:2, Psa 63:6, Psa 119:97 and Psa 143:5 meditation is a murmured dwelling on God, his law and his works, done by day and night and in the night watches; it is the person's own and continual.

In Psa 77:12, Psa 119:15, Psa 119:23, Psa 119:27, Psa 119:48, Psa 119:78, Psa 119:148 and Psa 145:5 the meditating is a resolve, I will meditate, set on God's precepts, statutes, promise, works and deeds.
In Jos 1:8 the meditating is commanded: the Book of the Law is to be meditated on day and night instead of leaving the mouth.
In Jos 1:8 the meditating leads on in a chain: it is so that the person keeps to doing what is written, and then the way is made prosperous.

What the devout meditation is set on, where a verse names it: the Book of the Law and God's law, precepts, statutes, testimonies and promise, his works, deeds and the splendor of his majesty, and God himself in Psa 63:6. Verses: Jos 1:8, Psa 1:2, Psa 63:6, Psa 77:12, Psa 119:15, Psa 119:23, Psa 119:27, Psa 119:48, Psa 119:78, Psa 119:97, Psa 119:99, Psa 119:148, Psa 143:5, Psa 145:5.
In Psa 1:2, Psa 119:48 and Psa 119:97 the meditation is a pursuit of its object: delight in the law and love of the commandments come just before the meditating on them.
In Psa 63:6, Psa 77:3, Psa 77:6 and Psa 143:5 remembering comes first and meditating follows: of God, of a song in the night, of the days of old.
The meditating is set in the night in Psa 63:6, Psa 77:6 and Psa 119:148: on the bed, in the night, in the watches of the night with the eyes awake.
In Psa 119:23 and Psa 119:78 the meditating goes on against opponents: princes plot against the servant, the insolent wrong him with falsehood, and he meditates on the statutes and precepts.
In Psa 77:3 and Psa 77:6 the meditating goes with distress: when the speaker meditates his spirit faints, beside his moaning; after he meditates in his heart his spirit searches.
The heart is where the meditation and the pondering take place in Psa 19:14, Psa 49:3, Pro 15:28 and Luk 2:19: the meditation of the heart beside the words of the mouth, the heart that ponders.
In Pro 15:28 the outward act the pondering serves is an answer: the righteous heart ponders how to answer, set against the mouth of the wicked that pours out evil.
In Psa 38:12 the same verb of meditating is set on harm: the ones who seek the speaker's life turn treachery over in thought through the whole day, beside their talk of ruin.
In Luk 2:19 and Act 10:19 the pondering is held within: Mary treasures the things and ponders them in her heart, and Peter ponders the vision while the Spirit speaks to him.
In Pro 5:21 the pondering is the Lord's: he weighs all the paths of a man, whose ways are before his eyes.
In Gen 24:63 the musing is solitary, in the open field toward evening, with no object named.
In 1Ki 18:27 musing is named as a withdrawn state, one of several Elijah ascribes in mockery to the god of the others: musing, a journey, sleep.
In Job 15:4 the meditation before God is hindered, in the same charge as setting aside the fear of God: the act is held back, not pursued.
In Psa 19:14 and Psa 104:34 the meditation is offered to the Lord: it is to be acceptable in his sight and pleasing to him, with the words of the mouth and the rejoicing in him.
In Psa 119:99 the meditation is the ground of understanding: because the testimonies are his meditation, the speaker understands more than his teachers.
In 2Cor 5:16 the once regarded is a former knowing of Christ by the standard of the flesh: the person did it in the past, and the verse reports it as given up.
In 2Cor 5:16 the flesh is the standard by which the knowing took account of Christ, and the same standard is now set aside for everyone: the working is measured by what it judges by.
In 2Cor 5:16 the knowing by the flesh is refused from now on: no longer, no one.

In Act 17:2, Act 17:17, Act 18:4, Act 18:19, Act 19:8, Act 19:9 and Act 24:25 reasoning is an operation of speech: one person argues a matter with hearers, from the Scriptures and with persuading beside it, in the synagogue, the market and the hall; it is done, and done again over Sabbaths, days and months.
What the spoken reasoning is directed at, where the verses give it: the Scriptures in Act 17:2, the kingdom of God in Act 19:8, and righteousness, self-control and the judgment to come in Act 24:25.
In Act 24:25 the reasoning about righteousness, self-control and judgment is followed by the hearer's alarm and by his putting it off: Felix sends Paul away for the present and will call him later.

In Act 19:9 the hearers' hardening, their unbelief and their speaking evil of the Way come before the reasoning moves: Paul withdraws, takes the disciples with him, and reasons daily in the hall of Tyrannus.
In Luk 9:47 and 1Cor 13:11 reasoning is held within the person and addressed to no one: in the hearts of those of Luk 9:47, and as the reckoning of a child in 1Cor 13:11.
In Luk 9:47 the reasoning held in the hearts is known by Jesus, and he answers it with an act, not a word: he takes a child and sets him by his side.
In 1Cor 13:11 like a child gives the reasoning its quality: a child's way of reckoning, set with a child's speaking and thinking, and given up when the speaker became a man.

In Dan 4:34 and Dan 4:36 the king's reason returns after he lifts his eyes to heaven, and blessing, praise and honor of the Most High follow; with it his majesty and splendor return and he is set again in his kingdom.

In Jam 3:17 open to reason is a quality of the wisdom from above, set among pure, peaceable, gentle, full of mercy, impartial and sincere: a readiness to yield to another, given as a trait of that wisdom.

In 1Pe 3:15 the outward act is a spoken defense of the hope, given to anyone who asks: the readiness is constant, the honoring of Christ in the heart is set before it, and it is made with gentleness and respect.
In Isa 1:18 the Lord calls the people to reason the case out together, and what the reasoning concerns is their sins, red as scarlet, to be made white.
In Mar 12:24 being wrong rests on not knowing: those Jesus answers are in error because they lack knowledge of the Scriptures and of what God can do.
In Job 1:9 and Pro 3:30 the ground of an act is denied or questioned: whether the fear of God is for nothing, and contending with one who has done no harm.
In Mar 8:33 setting the mind on the things of God is denied of Peter: the act is stated as not done, and the mind is set elsewhere.
In Mar 8:33 what the mind is set on is one of two opposites: the things of God or the things of man.
In Mar 8:33 the set of mind is a refusal of the things of God in favour of the things of man, as the verse states it.
In Mar 8:33 the set of mind is named in a rebuke: Jesus turns, sees the disciples, and rebukes Peter, so the correction is spoken in the hearing of the others.

In Luk 2:44, Joh 11:31, Joh 20:15, Act 14:19, Act 16:27 and Act 27:13 supposing is a belief about a present fact, taken up without testing: the boy is in the group, Mary goes to the tomb, the man is the gardener, Paul is dead, the prisoners have fled, the purpose is gained. The person does it, and an act rests on it.

The supposing leads straight into an act in the same verse: the parents travel a day and then search in Luk 2:44, the Jews follow Mary in Joh 11:31, Mary speaks to the one she takes for the gardener in Joh 20:15, the crowds drag Paul out in Act 14:19, the jailer draws his sword to kill himself in Act 16:27, the sailors weigh anchor in Act 27:13.

Where the supposing is acted on it is a pursuit of its content: in Joh 11:31 the Jews go after Mary to the tomb they suppose she goes to, in Luk 2:44 the parents go on a day's journey as if the boy were with them, in Act 27:13 the sailors sail on as if their purpose were gained.

What the supposing rests on is named in some verses: in Act 16:27 the jailer sees the prison doors open, in Joh 20:15 Mary is weeping and seeking the body, in Act 14:19 the crowds have stoned Paul. The supposing is taken from what is seen or felt, not from what is so.

In 1Cor 8:2, 1Ti 6:5, Luk 7:43 and Joh 21:25 a view is held: that one knows something, that godliness is gain, which debtor would love more, how many books the world could hold. The person holds it as a judgment of his own.
In 2Sa 13:32, 2Sa 13:33 and Jam 1:7 the view is forbidden: the king is not to suppose all his sons dead or take it to heart, and the doubter is not to suppose he will receive from the Lord.

Where the view is forbidden it is a refusal: in 2Sa 13:32 and 2Sa 13:33 the king is to refuse the view that all his sons are dead, and in Jam 1:7 the doubter is to refuse the expectation of receiving.

In Act 13:25, Rom 2:3 and Jam 4:5 the view is asked of the hearers: what they suppose John to be, whether the one who judges supposes he will escape God's judgment, whether the readers suppose the Scripture speaks for nothing. The question tests the view it asks about.

The verse tests the view and corrects or confirms it: in Act 2:15 the men are not drunk, since it is the third hour; in Act 13:25 John says he is not the one; in 2Sa 13:32 and 2Sa 13:33 Amnon alone is dead; in Luk 7:43 Jesus says Simon has judged rightly.

In 1Cor 8:2, Rom 2:3 and Jam 1:7 the view is about oneself: that one knows, that one will escape judgment, that one will receive. Each verse sets the view against what is so: not yet knowing as one ought, God's judgment, the doubter's lack.

The view is set in the heart or mind: in 2Sa 13:33 the king is not to take the report to heart, in 1Ti 6:5 the false view is held by people depraved in mind, and in Pro 18:11 the rich man's wealth is a wall in his own imagination.

In Pro 18:11 and Act 17:29 imagination is the mind's own picture or device: the rich man pictures his wealth as a high wall, and human art and imagination form an image of gold or stone. What is pictured is not the thing itself.
In Act 17:29 and 1Ti 6:5 the false view is about God: the divine being is thought like an image formed by man, and godliness is taken for a way to gain. The verses deny both.
In Psa 41:7 imagining is devising harm: those who hate the psalmist plan the worst for him while they whisper together.
The devising of Psa 41:7 is a pursuit of harm against a person, and it comes from hatred: all who hate the psalmist whisper and plan the worst against him.

In Gen 18:28 to Gen 18:32 suppose is a particle that puts a case, not an act of the mind: Abraham puts lower numbers of righteous one after another, asks the Lord not to be angry, and each case is answered by the Lord's not destroying. In Eze 18:14 the prophet puts the case of a son who sees his father's sins and does not do them.

In Rom 8:5 and Rom 8:6 the mind is set on something: a person directs his mind to an object and holds it there, so that the mind-set becomes his frame of thought. It is stated as done by those who live one way or the other.
In Rom 8:5 and Rom 8:6 what the mind is set on is one of two opposites: the flesh and its things, or the Spirit and its things.

In Rom 8:5 the way a person lives, by the flesh or by the Spirit, goes with where the mind is set, and in Rom 8:6 the set of mind is itself death, or life and peace: living, the set of mind and its outcome are joined.
In Rom 8:5 and Rom 8:6 the setting of the mind is a pursuit of its object, in either direction: toward the flesh or toward the Spirit.

In thirty-five verses of narrative and saying (Gen 20:11, 1Sa 18:11, 2Ki 5:11, Psa 64:5, Jer 3:19, Luk 12:17 and the others) the thought is inner speech: the person says a sentence within, and the sentence is the thought, usually about what another will do or what will follow. The person does it, in the first person.

The thought held is shown wrong in the verse or the account: Abraham's no fear of God in Gen 20:11, Samuel before Eliab in 1Sa 16:6, Naaman's expectation in 2Ki 5:11, the father's in Judg 15:2, the Lord's hope of return in Jer 3:7, the ghost in Mar 6:49, the spirit in Luk 24:37, sleep for death in Joh 11:13, the errand in Joh 13:29, the vision in Act 12:9, more pay in Mat 20:10, the gift bought in Act 8:20.

Fear comes first and the thought gives its reason in Gen 31:31, Exo 2:14, 2Sa 14:15 and Job 32:6; in Neh 6:9 the enemies mean to frighten, expecting the work to stop, and in Luk 24:37 the startled disciples take what they see for a spirit.
In Dan 4:19, Dan 5:6, Dan 5:10 and Dan 7:28 the thoughts themselves alarm the one who has them, and the color of the face changes: the thoughts work on the person and show in the body.

The heart, or the mind, is named as where the thoughts are: in Gen 6:5, Deu 15:9, 1Ch 29:18, Isa 10:7, Jer 4:14, Mat 9:4, Mat 15:19, Mar 7:21, Luk 1:51, Luk 2:35, Luk 5:22 and Dan 7:28 they are of the heart, lodge within it, come out of it or are revealed from it; in Eze 11:5, Eze 20:32, Eze 38:10 and Dan 2:30 they come into the mind.

Thoughts arise and lead out into acts: in Eze 38:10 thoughts come into the mind and a scheme is devised, in Dan 2:29 they come to the king in bed, and in Mat 15:19 and Mar 7:21 evil thoughts come out of the heart first, before murder, adultery and the rest.

The thoughts of people are what the Lord knows, searches and discerns: in Psa 94:11, Psa 139:2, Psa 139:23, 1Ch 28:9, 1Cor 3:20, Eze 11:5 and Isa 66:18 he knows them, and in Heb 4:12 the word discerns them with the heart's intentions. The thoughts lie open to him.
In Mat 9:4, Mat 12:25, Luk 5:22, Luk 6:8 and Luk 11:17 Jesus knows or perceives the thoughts of those around him and answers them: their thoughts are what his knowing reaches.
In 1Cor 2:11 only the spirit of a person, within him, knows his thoughts, and in Ecc 10:20 even what is cursed in thought may be carried abroad: the thought is inward and yet not hidden.

The Lord himself thinks: his thoughts toward his people are many and deep in Psa 40:5 and Psa 92:5, precious to the psalmist in Psa 139:17, above man's in Isa 55:8 and Isa 55:9 and unknown to the nations in Mic 4:12; he thought to give Israel a land in Jer 3:19, he will do to Israel as he thought to do to the nations in Num 33:56, and he takes thought for the poor in Psa 40:17.

What the thoughts are set on is evil in Gen 6:5, Job 21:27, Psa 56:5, Psa 64:5, Pro 15:26, Isa 59:7, Jer 4:14, Eze 38:10, Mat 9:4, Mat 15:19, Mar 7:21 and Jam 2:4: wrong against another, iniquity, an evil scheme, judging with evil.
In Isa 55:7 the unrighteous man is called to forsake his thoughts, and in Jer 4:14 Jerusalem is asked how long wicked thoughts will lodge within her: the thoughts are to be given up.
In Isa 55:7 forsaking the thoughts leads on: the man returns to the Lord, who has compassion and pardons abundantly.

Thinking is planning or intending in Isa 10:7, Jer 23:27, Dan 7:25, 1Sa 18:25, Job 6:26, 2Ch 13:8, 2Sa 21:16 and Phili 1:17: to destroy nations, to make the people forget the name, to change times and law, to make David fall, to withstand the Lord's kingdom, to kill David, to afflict Paul. The person intends an act.

The thought is carried into the deed in the same verse: in Num 33:56 the Lord will do as he thought, in 1Sa 18:21 Saul gives his daughter as a snare, in Gen 32:20 Jacob sends the present to appease Esau, and in 1Sa 27:11 David leaves none alive.

Giving thought is attention of the mind turned to a matter: the psalmist thinks on his ways in Psa 119:59, recalls the Lord's rules in Psa 119:52, dwells on his steadfast love in Psa 48:9, and tries to understand in Psa 73:16; the prudent and the upright give thought to their steps in Pro 14:15 and Pro 21:29; the people of faith did not keep the land in mind in Heb 11:15.

Attention leads on: in Psa 119:59 thinking on his ways turns the psalmist's feet to the testimonies, in Psa 119:52 thinking of the rules brings comfort, in Psa 73:16 the thinking wearies until he goes into the sanctuary, and in Heb 11:15 keeping the land in mind would have given the chance to return.
In Phili 4:8 the thinking is commanded and given its objects: whatever is true, honorable, just, pure, lovely and worthy of praise.
In Lam 1:9 Jerusalem took no thought of her future, and her fall followed; in Ecc 9:10 there is no thought in Sheol. The want of thought is named as a lack.

Thinking is a judgment of what is so or fitting: Judah takes the woman for a prostitute in Gen 38:15, a thing is unclean to the one who counts it so in Rom 14:14, the raising of the dead is judged incredible in Act 26:8, Paul judges what is needful in 2Cor 9:5 and Phili 2:25, and what seems best in someone's eyes decides in Num 36:6, 2Sa 3:19, Jer 40:4 and Jer 40:5.

The thought is turned on oneself: in 1Cor 3:18, 1Cor 10:12, 1Cor 14:37, Gal 6:3, Phili 3:4, Jam 1:26 and Luk 8:18 a person thinks he is wise, stands, is a prophet, is something, has grounds for confidence, is religious or has what he has; in Rom 12:3 one is not to think of oneself more highly than one ought.

In Gal 6:3, Jam 1:26 and 1Cor 3:18 the self-view leads to self-deceit: the one who rates himself as something, being nothing, misleads himself, and the one who counts himself wise must first become a fool.

The thought is asked of the hearer in Mat 17:25, Mat 18:12, Mat 21:28, Mat 22:17, Mat 22:42, Luk 10:36, Joh 11:56, Luk 13:2, Luk 13:4, Heb 10:29, 2Ki 18:20 and Isa 36:5: what do you think, do you think. The question draws out a judgment the hearer forms.

The thought is forbidden or denied in Mat 5:17, Mat 10:34, Joh 5:45, Act 17:29, 2Cor 11:16, Est 4:13 and Isa 10:7: do not think, we ought not to think, let no one think, do not think to yourself, his heart does not so think. The verse corrects what would be thought.

Where the thought is set against God it is a refusal: in Psa 10:4 the wicked man's thoughts say there is no God, in Rom 1:21 those who knew God did not honor or thank him and became futile in thinking, in Psa 50:21 they thought God like themselves, in Eze 20:32 the thought is to be like the nations, and in 2Cor 10:5 every lofty opinion against the knowledge of God is pulled down.

Where the thought is turned toward God it is a pursuit: in Psa 139:23 the psalmist asks God to search and know his thoughts, in Psa 139:17 God's thoughts are precious to him, in Psa 48:9 the people dwell on his steadfast love, in 1Ch 29:18 David asks that such purposes be kept in the hearts of the people, and in Psa 119:59 the thinking turns the feet to the testimonies.

The thinking has a measure: mature or childish in 1Cor 14:20 and 1Cor 13:11, sober in Rom 12:3, the same mind or another in Phili 3:15, futile in Rom 1:21, and armed with Christ's mind in 1Pe 4:1. The words give the thinking its maturity or its emptiness.

In 2Cor 10:5 the thoughts are taken captive to obey Christ, and in 2Cor 11:3 Paul fears they will be led astray from devotion to him by deceit: the thoughts are what is either brought under Christ or drawn away.
In Job 32:6, Job 32:10 and Job 32:17 Elihu holds back his opinion out of fear and then declares it, and in Pro 18:2 the fool delights only in airing his: the view is held and spoken.

In Job 15:35, Isa 33:11 and Isa 59:4 what is conceived within is then born: trouble, chaff and mischief conceived, evil, stubble and iniquity brought forth. The figure joins what is formed within to what comes out.

In Pro 24:32, Ecc 2:11, Eze 18:28, Dan 7:8, Rom 4:19 and Mat 1:20 considering is attention set on a matter and taken in: the field looked over, the toil surveyed, the transgressions seen, the horns watched, the body faced, the things Joseph turned over. The person does it, and it comes before a turn, a verdict or a word from God.
In Job 1:8 and Job 2:3 the Lord asks Satan whether he has set his heart on Job: the considering is put as a question to another, and the heart is named as what is set on the person.
In Isa 53:8 the question who of his generation considered that he was cut off states that none gave it thought: the considering is denied of the servant's own generation.
In Eze 18:28 the considering leads a chain: the man considers, turns away from the transgressions he committed, and shall live and not die.
In Pro 24:32 the considering stands between seeing and being taught: the man sees the field, sets his heart on it, looks, and receives instruction.
In Ecc 2:11 the considering of all the work and toil ends in a verdict: all was vanity and nothing was gained.

Counting someone or something as a certain thing is the second act of the subgroup: in Heb 11:11, Heb 11:19, Heb 11:26, Pro 17:28, Neh 13:13, 2Ch 9:20, Mar 10:42, Luk 22:24, Gen 31:15, Psa 44:22, Rom 8:36, Lam 4:2 and Hos 8:12 a person, a people, a thing or God is counted faithful, able, greater, wise, reliable, nothing, rulers, the greatest, foreigners, sheep, pots or strange. It is a valuation that gives a standing.

In Heb 11:11, Heb 11:19, Heb 11:26 and Rom 4:19 the counting is done by faith and is set on God: the one who promised is counted faithful, God is counted able to raise the dead, reproach for Christ is counted above Egypt's treasures with the eye on the reward, and Abraham faces his own body without his faith weakening.

In Jer 24:5, Isa 29:17 and Rom 2:26 the counting is foreseen: the Lord will count the exiles good, the field shall be counted a forest, the uncircumcised who keeps the precepts will be counted as circumcised.

The counting is commanded or asked of people in Lev 19:23, 1Ti 6:1, 1Cor 4:1, 2Th 3:15, 1Sa 1:16 and 1Sa 25:25: fruit to be counted forbidden, masters worthy of honor, the apostles as servants of Christ, the disobedient not an enemy, Hannah not a worthless woman, Nabal not to be taken to heart.

Regard is given as a done act in 2Ki 3:14, Pro 12:10 and Psa 144:3: Elisha's regard for Jehoshaphat, the righteous man's knowing care for the life of his beast, and the Lord's regard for man, which the psalmist wonders at.

Regard is asked in Psa 74:20, Psa 80:14, 2Ch 6:19 and Psa 119:117: the Lord is asked to have regard for the covenant, the vine and his servant's prayer, and the psalmist asks to be held up so that he may have regard for the statutes. In Deu 9:27 the Lord is asked not to regard the people's stubbornness.

Regard withheld is a refusal in Gen 4:5, Job 35:13, Job 37:24, Lam 4:16, Psa 28:5, Isa 5:12, Job 34:27, Deu 33:9, Job 9:21, Isa 13:17, Isa 33:8, Exo 5:9 and 1Ki 10:21: God withholds it from Cain's offering, an empty cry, the conceited and a scattered people; people withhold it from God's works and ways; Levi from his kin, Job from himself, the Medes from silver, the land from man, the men from lying words, and Solomon's days from silver. The negator reaches the regard each time.

Where regard is given or sought it is a pursuit of its object: in Pro 12:10 the righteous reaches to the life of his beast, in 2Ki 3:14 Elisha acts for the king's sake, in Psa 119:117 the psalmist seeks lasting regard for the statutes, and in 2Ch 6:19 the Lord is asked to turn to the prayer.

In 1Sa 1:16, 1Sa 25:25 and Job 37:24 the regard is bound to worth: Hannah asks not to be counted worthless, Abigail asks that worthless Nabal not be taken to heart, and God withholds regard from the wise in their own conceit.
In 2Ch 6:19 and Job 35:13 regard goes with hearing: the Lord is asked to regard the prayer and listen to the cry, and an empty cry God neither hears nor regards.
In Job 34:27 turning aside from following God and having no regard for his ways are one fault, and in Psa 28:5 not regarding the Lord's works leads to being torn down and not built up.
In Deu 33:9 withholding regard from father and mother, disowning brothers and ignoring children stands with keeping the word and the covenant: the refusal is for the sake of what is kept.
In 2Cor 5:16 the regard by the standard of the flesh is given up: Paul once knew Christ that way and now takes account of no one by it.
In 1Cor 14:29 weighing in the mind is commanded: when two or three prophets have spoken, the others are to weigh what is said, judging and discerning it.
In Ecc 12:9 the wise Preacher weighs proverbs, with studying and arranging, as part of teaching the people knowledge: the weighing tests and orders what is learned.
